newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia, meets premier.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, recovering from pneumonia, meets premier.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin went to the Kremlin for the second time in a week on Tuesday, but reassuring official comments have done little to dispel speculation that he is not well enough to rule Russia.

The presidential press office said Yeltsin, who has been recovering from pneumonia in an official residence outside Moscow, met Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the Kremlin for just over an hour.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Kremlin sources as saying they discussed Monday's election in rebel Chechnya and the social and economic situation in Russia.
But newspapers, commenting on Yeltsin's decision on Monday to call off a trip to the Netherlands at short notice, said rumours about the president's health would not go away.
Yeltsin, who turns 66 on Saturday, has spent only a few days in the Kremlin since he won a second term in office last July. He was ill first with heart problems and then with pneumonia.

"A new wave of infernal rumours about the health of the president is inevitable, and they are becoming harder to refute," Sevodnya said in a front-page story which suggested that Yeltsin could be ill with some "third disease".
Sovietskaya Rossiya, one of the leading anti-government newspapers, published a cartoon showing a glowering president apparently steering the ship of state from his hospital bed.

The communist opposition in the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, has already launched an attempt to oust him on health grounds, although it admits the legal justification is shaky, given a constitution which gives the president strong powers.
Rivals, including former security chief Alexander Lebed, are jockying for position in case of an early vote.
Lebed told Reuters on Tuesday he was sure a presidential election would be held soon. "I am getting ready," he said.

Yeltsin has not been seen on television or in public since he fell ill with pneumonia over three weeks ago, a gap even longer than the two-week disappearance from public view after he had heart surgery on November 5.
There was, unusually for Russia, no television footage of his last visit to the Kremlin, which aides said took place on Wednesday, as the Duma debated a move to force him to quit.
Doctors have advised the president not to rush his return to work. But aides said last week that Yeltsin was raring to get back to the Kremlin.

"The president clearly has a huge, burning desire to return as soon as possible to carrying out his duties in full...and it is clear he has retained his characteristic political will," press spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said last Friday.

The Kremlin said on Monday that Yeltsin was cancelling a trip to the Netherlands because doctors had advised him not to fly. It would have been his first trip abroad since he visited China and Kazakhstan last April.
But a visit to Russia by French President Jacques Chirac would go ahead as planned on Sunday.
Yeltsin is planning to go to the United States in March for talks with President Bill Clinton, but final details have not yet been settled.
